criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access. The article introduces and describes the Municipal Drinking Water Database (MDWD), which links municipal-level public finance accounts, Census demographics, 2016 presidential vote share, city staffing and form of government, climate moisture, water source, and Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based water quality violations for municipally owned community water systems.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the database compiles broad institutional and regulatory variables (restricting the dataset to municipally owned community water systems, coding a binary mayor-led vs. council form-of-government variable, tracking municipal revenues/expenditures and staffing, and summing annual SDWA health-based violations), though these are presented only as descriptive summaries of a new data resource rather than tested as governance determinants of access; even if treated as touching governance under the plain reading, the paper still fails Criteria 1, 4, and 5 so plain_criterion2_decision is exclude. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, Criterion 2 is clearly not met (no): municipal utility ownership is a constant sample-inclusion filter (non-municipal and special-district systems are excluded rather than compared), mayor-led form of government is unanalysed macro-governance background reported only as a univariate descriptive statistic, and no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, administrative burden, tariff or cost-recovery rules, disconnection/enforcement, or regulatory rules governing access) is examined.
criterion_notes.c3: Compiles a secondary longitudinal unbalanced panel dataset (1997–2018) across 2,219 U.S. municipalities and reports quantitative descriptive statistics and illustrative temporal and regional patterns.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no outcome measuring water or sanitation service access, connection, coverage, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, household affordability, or disconnection/exclusion. The drinking-water system metrics in the database and illustrative analyses are limited to aggregate municipal water utility expenditures and revenues and annual counts of health-based SDWA water-quality violations (MCL, MRDL, and treatment-technique violations).
criterion_notes.c5: Although the municipality-level population (2,219 contiguous U.S. municipalities) and database linkage methods are clearly documented, this is a data-resource description paper presenting univariate summaries, spending trends, and an illustrative plot of regional climate moisture against per-capita water utility spending, with no identifiable study design testing a legal/governance exposure on a service-access outcome.

study_design: Database construction and description paper (unbalanced longitudinal panel dataset, 1997–2018, with illustrative descriptive statistics)
population_and_sample: 2,219 U.S. municipalities in the 48 contiguous states with at least 10,000 residents in the 2000 Census that own and operate a community water system serving at least 8,000 people (collectively serving approximately 139 million residents), tracked from 1997 to 2018 (unit of analysis: municipality)
exposure: not reported (database compiles municipal finances, mayor-led vs. council form of government, municipal FTEs, demographics, 2016 Democratic vote share, water source, and Climate Moisture Index; illustrative bivariate comparison examines regional Climate Moisture Index)
outcome: Aggregate municipal water utility spending and revenue, general municipal fiscal indicators, and annual count of Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based water quality violations (no household or community service-access outcome reported)
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). This article is a data-resource description introducing the Municipal Drinking Water Database (MDWD) for 2,219 U.S. municipalities with municipally owned community water systems (1997–2018). Neither the compiled database variables nor the illustrative descriptive analyses measure household or community water service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, household tariff affordability, or disconnection/exclusion (failing Criteria 1 and 4); instead, the drinking-water metrics are limited to aggregate municipal utility revenues/expenditures and Safe Drinking Water Act health-based water quality violations. It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification (municipal ownership is a fixed sample-selection criterion with no comparison group, and mayor-vs.-council form of government is unanalysed macro-governance background) and Criterion 5 (descriptive database overview with no governance-exposure to access-outcome analysis), so it is excluded under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
